item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — “single training run.”** A developer could divide training across several nominal runs, checkpoints, subsidiaries, or stages, keeping each run below \(10^{26}\) operations even if the combined process exceeds the threshold.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — incomplete computation measure.** The bill does not say which operations count, how mixed-precision operations are converted, or whether data processing, failed runs, reinforcement learning, fine-tuning, and other post-training work are included. That makes the threshold both gameable and difficult to prove.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — exact-threshold exclusion.** Because the definition says “greater than” \(10^{26}\), a model trained using exactly that amount is not covered.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — model-versus-system mismatch.** This paragraph automatically covers only an AI “model,” while section 3 regulates a covered “system.” Companies could argue that applications, model ensembles, modified copies, or systems built around a covered model are legally distinct from the model itself.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — derivatives and fine-tunes.** A powerful model produced by fine-tuning or modifying an existing model may involve less than \(10^{26}\) operations in its own training run. Unless the Secretary separately designates it under paragraph (B), it may fall outside the definition.

6. **Section 2(1)(B) — unidentified Secretary.** The bill never defines “the Secretary.” The reference to the Department of Commerce in section 4 suggests the Commerce Secretary, but a court or regulated party should not have to infer which official holds this authority.

7. **Section 2(1)(B) — vague capability standard.** “Capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks” does not identify the relevant humans, tasks, tests, degree of superiority, or conditions of use. That uncertainty invites due-process vagueness challenges and inconsistent designations.

8. **Section 2(1)(B) — no designation process.** The bill gives no procedure for testing systems, issuing determinations, notifying developers, handling confidential information, or obtaining administrative or judicial review. It also does not say whether a determination is prospective or can make earlier conduct unlawful.

9. **Section 2(2) — narrow definition of U.S. person.** The definition omits permanent residents and many U.S.-organized entities that are not corporations, including partnerships, trusts, and some limited-liability companies. It may also leave foreign subsidiaries of U.S. corporations outside the extraterritorial prohibition.

10. **Section 2(3) — “advanced AI chips” undefined.** The registry cannot be applied consistently because the bill supplies no performance, architecture, age, or export-control standard for deciding which chips qualify.

11. **Section 2(3) — facility-counting loopholes.** “Containing more than 50,000” excludes facilities with exactly 50,000 chips and permits operators to divide chips among nominally separate facilities, buildings, or campuses. The bill does not define the boundaries of a “data center” or address temporarily installed, leased, inactive, or remotely pooled chips.

12. **Section 3(a) — uncertain territorial language.** “Any person in the United States” is unclear when the actor, company, equipment, personnel, and cloud resources are in different countries. The bill does not specify whether jurisdiction turns on physical presence, incorporation, control, computing location, or where the system is made available.

13. **Section 3(a) — undefined regulated acts.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” are not defined. Uncertainty about whether they include fine-tuning, testing, hosting, copying weights, providing an API, internal use, open-source release, or integration into another product would complicate enforcement.

14. **Section 3(a) — significant conduct is not expressly prohibited.** The provision does not expressly prohibit possessing, buying, selling, licensing, importing, exporting, financing, or transferring a covered system or its weights. Actors could structure transactions so that no one entity clearly performs one of the three prohibited acts.

15. **Section 3(a) — service-provider gap.** Cloud providers, chip lessors, financiers, and data-center operators may enable prohibited training without themselves “training, developing, or deploying” the system. The civil provisions contain no express aiding-and-abetting, facilitation, or control-person liability.

16. **Section 3(a) — uncertain application to government.** The prohibition applies to a “person,” but the bill neither defines that term nor expressly includes federal agencies and other governmental bodies. Governments may therefore be outside the ban even though their contractors are covered.

17. **Section 3(b) — unlimited grandfather clause.** Any system “whose training began” before enactment is exempt, with no requirement that meaningful training occurred or that it finish by a deadline. A company could begin a token training step before enactment and claim protection for a much larger project completed years later.

18. **Section 3(b) — unclear scope of grandfathering.** The bill does not say whether retraining, major architectural changes, new versions, fine-tunes, or systems derived from a grandfathered model remain the same “covered AI system.” It also appears to exempt not merely completion of training but all later development and deployment of the grandfathered system.

19. **Section 3(b) and Section 8 — 180-day rush window.** The Act does not take effect for 180 days, but the grandfather date is the earlier date of enactment. Although projects begun after enactment would not be grandfathered, section 3 would not yet be operative, creating uncertainty over whether work conducted during that window is lawful and whether it must stop on the effective date.

20. **Section 3(c) — broad safety-evaluation exception.** “Activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation” has no limits on scale, duration, participants, security, or permissible deployment. A company could characterize ordinary development or even public deployment as producing safety information.

21. **Section 3(c) — subjective and mixed purposes.** The bill does not require advance approval or independent verification of the asserted safety purpose, and it does not address activities having both safety and commercial objectives. Enforcement could turn on difficult evidence about a company’s stated intent.

22. **Section 4(a) — “operator” undefined.** Ownership, operation, leasing, and technical control may be divided among several entities. Without a rule identifying the responsible operator, each could contend that another party had the registration duty.

23. **Section 4 — registry does not cover all relevant computing.** Only facilities exceeding the chip-count threshold must register, even though covered models can be trained through distributed computing across many smaller facilities or foreign facilities. Conversely, the registry does not itself prohibit a registered facility from conducting prohibited work.

24. **Section 4(b) — reporting obligation is indeterminate.** “Describing the computing workloads” does not establish the required detail, format, measurement method, submission date, record-retention period, or treatment of trade secrets. Operators could satisfy it with descriptions too general to reveal covered training.

25. **Sections 4 and 5 — no penalty for registry violations.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3. Failure to register, report, certify accurately, or submit reports on time therefore has no express civil or criminal consequence under the Act.

26. **Sections 4 and 5 — inadequate investigative machinery.** The bill grants no inspection, audit, subpoena, recordkeeping, chip-tracking, or information-demand authority. Because training-compute records are generally held by the regulated companies, proving a violation could be especially difficult.

27. **Section 5(a) — no enforcement mechanism or designated enforcer.** The bill does not identify which agency or official assesses civil penalties, whether the Justice Department must sue, what process applies, or whether injunctions are available. It also creates no express authority to stop an ongoing training run quickly.

28. **Section 5(a) — daily penalty ambiguity.** It is unclear what constitutes a “day” of violation for instantaneous acts such as releasing weights or initiating a deployment, and whether continued availability creates a new violation each day. The “not more than” formulation also supplies no minimum penalty or factors for setting the amount.

29. **Section 5(a) and Section 8 — conflicting timing provisions.** Section 5 purports to cover violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 says the Act takes effect 180 days later. Conduct during that interval cannot clearly violate a prohibition that is not yet effective, making the penalty language confusing and potentially vulnerable to challenge.

30. **Section 5(b) — “willfully” undefined in context.** Courts use different willfulness standards depending on the statute. The bill does not clarify whether prosecutors must prove knowledge of the law, knowledge that the system met the technical definition, or only intentional performance of the underlying acts.

31. **Section 5 — no express treatment of attempts and civil facilitation.** The bill does not address attempted violations or expressly impose civil liability on those who direct, assist, or conspire in prohibited activity. Some general criminal doctrines may apply, but the civil reach is particularly uncertain.

32. **Section 6 — largely nonbinding international provision.** The Secretary of State need only “seek to negotiate”; there is no requirement to conclude, sign, or implement an agreement and no consequence for failure. “Equivalent” prohibitions are also undefined.

33. **Section 6 — offshore displacement remains possible.** Until an international agreement is adopted, foreign companies acting abroad remain outside the prohibition, as do some foreign affiliates of U.S. companies. That creates an incentive to move development, computing, or corporate control offshore.

34. **Section 7(a) — no required National Academies report.** The provision conditions an end to the prohibition on “a report” but does not direct anyone to request, fund, or complete that report, specify its contents, or set a deadline.

35. **Section 7(a) — uncertain termination standard.** “Congress, acting on a report,” and “can be developed safely” lack defined procedures or safety criteria. It is unclear how closely the joint resolution must follow the report or what findings it must contain.

36. **Section 7(a) and (b) — competing duration rules.** Subsection (a) suggests the prohibition persists until Congress makes a safety finding, but subsection (b) ends the entire Act after ten years regardless of any finding. The sunset therefore overrides the ostensibly safety-based duration rule.

37. **Section 7(b) — effect on pending matters unclear.** The Act contains no savings clause preserving accrued penalties, pending cases, reporting records, or investigations after sunset. Defendants could argue that expiration cuts off enforcement for earlier violations.

38. **Act-wide — no rulemaking authority or update mechanism.** The bill does not expressly authorize regulations to resolve technical questions, update the compute or chip thresholds, or respond to changes in hardware and training methods. Fixed numerical and undefined technological terms could quickly become obsolete.

39. **Act-wide — no severability clause.** If a court invalidates a central definition, delegation, or application of the prohibition, the absence of a severability provision creates additional uncertainty about whether the remainder of the Act survives.
